title: Builder Pattern
tagline: Construct complex objects step by step with a fluent API — solving the telescoping constructor problem and separating what is built from how it is assembled.

sections.content:
**Imagine you are calling a constructor with twelve arguments.** You type `new HttpRequest('https://api.example.com', 'POST', null, null, null, 5000, true, null, null, 3, null, 'application/json')` and a cold sweat runs down your back — which `null` is the proxy setting? Which is the auth token? Which is the cache policy? If you pass the arguments in the wrong order, the program compiles fine and fails silently at runtime in a way that is nearly impossible to diagnose.

This is the **telescoping constructor anti-pattern**: a constructor with so many optional parameters that callers must fill in a grid of positional nulls just to express a simple intent. The moment you add a thirteenth parameter, every single call site in the codebase becomes a potential breaking change.

**The Builder pattern solves this head-on.** Instead of a single overloaded constructor, you provide a companion `Builder` object that exposes one *named setter method* per configurable field. Each setter stores its value and returns `this`, enabling a **fluent (chainable) API**: `new RequestBuilder('https://api.example.com').method('POST').timeout(5000).retry(3).build()`. The final `.build()` call validates the accumulated configuration and produces the real, immutable object.

The pattern has three main participants: the **Builder** (which accumulates configuration), the **Product** (the complex object being constructed, typically immutable), and the optional **Director** (which encodes common construction recipes so teams do not have to remember the correct sequence every time).

In the JavaScript ecosystem, the Builder pattern is everywhere once you know what to look for. `knex` and `TypeORM`'s `QueryBuilder` are textbook builders (`.select().from().where().orderBy().limit().execute()`). `supertest` builds HTTP assertions step by step. Mongoose query chains, `jest`'s `expect` matchers, and most test-data factory libraries all implement the same pattern. Understanding Builder not only helps you write better APIs — it makes every query library you touch immediately legible.

sections.caption: The four participants of the Builder pattern. The Director is optional — it encodes reusable recipes using the Builder interface. ConcreteBuilder accumulates configuration and produces the immutable Product on build(). Clients can call the builder directly or through the Director.

sections.title: A Custom Sandwich Order at the Deli Counter
sections.content:
At a deli, you do not hand the server a printed slip with thirty checkbox columns and hope they decode your intent. You direct the assembly *step by step*, out loud: 'sourdough bread — turkey — extra swiss — no onion — chipotle mayo — yes, toasted.' Each sentence is a builder step. The server (the Builder) remembers every choice as the order accumulates. When you say 'that is it,' they assemble and hand over the finished sandwich (the Product). The sandwich is immutable once it reaches you — you eat it, you do not disassemble and rebuild it.

Now imagine the lunch-rush expert behind the counter — someone who has made thousands of sandwiches. When a regular walks in and says 'the usual Classic Club,' the expert does not ask for every ingredient: they run through a memorised sequence: white bread, turkey, bacon, lettuce, tomato, mayo. That expert is the **Director** — they encode a known recipe and execute it by calling the builder steps in the right order so the customer does not have to.

The key insight: at no point does the customer need to know whether the bread goes in first or last. The builder handles the assembly. The customer expresses *intent* — not *procedure*.

sections.title: The Telescoping Constructor: Understanding the Problem First
sections.content:
Before studying the solution, it is worth understanding the problem deeply. There are three common (bad) approaches to objects with many optional parameters, and each has a specific failure mode.

**Approach 1: Overloaded constructors.** Provide multiple constructors, each accepting a different number of parameters. This works until you have fifteen combinations — at which point maintaining fifteen constructors is itself a bug factory. JavaScript does not have native overloading at all, so developers fake it with `arguments.length` checks, which is even messier.

**Approach 2: Positional 'telescoping' parameters.** A single constructor accepts all parameters: `new Request(url, method, body, headers, timeout, retries, auth, proxy, cachePolicy, encoding, redirect, keepAlive)`. Callers pad unused parameters with `null` or `undefined`. When you read the call site a month later, you cannot tell which positional null is which field without counting. Adding a new parameter in the middle breaks every call site in the codebase.

**Approach 3: Mutable setter methods.** Create the object with a minimal constructor, then call setters: `const r = new Request(url); r.setTimeout(5000); r.setRetries(3);`. This is better, but it leaves the object in a partially-constructed, mutable state. Any code that receives the object before all setters are called sees an invalid object. You cannot enforce required fields or cross-field constraints.

**The Builder solution** retains the step-by-step ergonomics of approach 3 but solves both of its problems: the Product is only created (and validated) at the very end inside `build()`, so it is always either absent or fully valid. The builder is the intermediate mutable scratch-pad; the Product is the immutable result.

sections.title: The Four Participants in Detail
sections.content:
**Builder (interface or abstract class)** — declares the interface with one method per construction step plus a `build()` terminal method. Every setter method returns the builder itself (`this` or the builder type), enabling chaining. In dynamically-typed languages like JavaScript, the Builder is often implied rather than explicitly declared as an interface.

**ConcreteBuilder** — the class you actually instantiate. It maintains a mutable internal configuration object (or individual private fields). Each setter method updates one field of that config and returns `this`. The `build()` method performs validation, then passes the completed configuration to the Product's constructor. If validation fails, `build()` throws a descriptive error — *before* the Product is ever created.

**Product** — the complex object being constructed. In well-designed builders, the Product is immutable: its constructor accepts the final configuration, assigns all fields, and calls `Object.freeze()` (or the equivalent in the host language). There are no setter methods on the Product. This is a critical design decision: immutability guarantees that if a Product instance exists, it passed validation. You can pass it across async boundaries, store it in a cache, and share it between threads without defensive copies.

**Director (optional)** — knows the correct sequence and combination of builder calls for specific, commonly-needed objects. It receives the builder as a constructor argument (dependency injection) and exposes named methods like `buildAuthenticatedPost()` or `buildHealthCheckRequest()`. The Director decouples the *what* (the named preset) from the *how* (the exact sequence of builder calls). Teams use Directors to share construction recipes without copy-pasting builder chains across the codebase.

**Fluent API mechanics in depth:** returning `this` from each setter is not magic — it is a simple convention. The chain `builder.a(1).b(2).c(3)` is syntactic sugar for three sequential method calls on the same object. Each call mutates the builder's private state and hands back the builder so the next call can be chained immediately. The only time you do *not* chain is when you want to branch: build two variants from a partially-configured builder by calling `build()` twice, or by cloning the builder mid-chain.

The `clone()` method enables branching — building two variants from one partially-configured base, a pattern common in test suites. The Director shows how named presets eliminate repeated builder chains across team code.

sections.title: Immutability of the Product: Why It Matters
sections.content:
The Product being immutable is not an aesthetic choice — it is a correctness guarantee. Consider what happens without immutability:

```js
const req = builder.build();
req.method = 'DELETE';  // oops — bypasses all validation
sendRequest(req);       // DELETE was never validated
```

With `Object.freeze()`, that assignment silently fails in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode. The Product's constructor validated the config; freezing it ensures that validation remains the single source of truth for the object's lifetime.

**Thread safety and async boundaries.** In environments with shared state (Node.js worker threads, browser shared workers, or any language with real threads), immutable objects can be passed across boundaries without defensive copies. Since no thread can mutate the object, no synchronisation is needed. This is not hypothetical: request configuration objects in HTTP servers are frequently passed between middleware, request handlers, and interceptors across async hops. An immutable config is safe to pass by reference.

**Cache keys.** Immutable objects can safely be used as cache keys or lookup tokens. If the object could be mutated after cache insertion, the cache key would drift from the stored value — a particularly nasty bug. Several query builder libraries (like Apollo's normalized cache) rely on immutability of query descriptor objects for this exact reason.

**The builder as a mutable scratch-pad.** The division of labor is clean: the **builder** is deliberately mutable and lives only during construction. The **product** is deliberately immutable and lives for the rest of its lifetime. Never expose the builder's internal config object as the product — always copy it (as the `build()` method does with `{ ...this.#config }`).

sections.title: Validation Strategies Inside build()
sections.content:
The `build()` method is more powerful than it first appears. Because it has access to the *entire accumulated configuration*, it can enforce rules that are impossible to check at the individual setter level.

**Required field checks.** Check that mandatory fields are present: `if (!this.#config.url) throw new Error('url is required')`. This is the fundamental use case — ensure the product is never created with missing data.

**Cross-field constraints.** Some rules span multiple fields:
- HTTP: `method === 'GET'` and `body !== null` is invalid.
- Date range: `endDate` must be after `startDate`.
- Pagination: `pageSize` must be positive if `page > 0`.
- Auth: if `authType === 'oauth'`, then `oauthToken` is required; if `authType === 'apiKey'`, then `apiKey` is required.

None of these can be checked in individual setters because a setter only sees one field at a time. `build()` sees all of them simultaneously.

**Type coercions and normalisation.** `build()` is a good place to normalise data: convert `method` to uppercase, trim whitespace from `url`, parse a string `timeout` into a number, canonicalise header names to lowercase. The Product always receives clean, canonical data.

**Conditional defaults.** Some defaults depend on other fields: if `retries > 0` and no `retryDelay` was set, default `retryDelay` to `1000 * retries`. These computed defaults are trivial in `build()` but impossible in individual setters.

**Error message quality.** Because `build()` is the validation gate, it is the place to write developer-friendly error messages: `'method must be one of: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE — received "RETRIEVE"'`. These messages appear at the exact moment of misuse, with full context, unlike constructor errors that appear at runtime with a cryptic stack trace.

sections.title: The Director: Encoding Team Knowledge
sections.content:
The Director is the most misunderstood participant. Many tutorials present it as mandatory; in practice it is **optional and powerful** when used for the right purpose.

**When you need a Director:** your team has several developers who all need to build the same kind of complex object (an authenticated API request, a test database fixture, a standard email notification). Without a Director, each developer writes their own builder chain — and they will inevitably differ. One developer forgets `retry(3)`. Another uses the wrong `Content-Type`. A third sets `timeout(0)` accidentally.

A Director centralises these recipes: `director.buildAuthenticatedPost(body, token)` always produces a correctly-configured request. The Director is team-wide knowledge encoded as code.

**The Director does NOT create the Builder.** A common misconception is that the Director owns the builder. In fact, the client creates the builder and passes it to the Director. This means the Director works with any builder that implements the correct interface — you can swap `HttpRequestBuilder` for `MockRequestBuilder` in tests without changing the Director at all.

**The Director vs. a factory method.** A factory method (`RequestFactory.createAuthPost(body, token)`) looks similar from the outside. The difference: a factory method hides the construction mechanism entirely and returns a product directly. The Director uses a builder explicitly, which means clients can still customise after calling a Director method (they have the builder), or combine multiple Director steps. The Director also clearly signals 'there is a multi-step construction process here' — useful architectural documentation.

**Real-world Director equivalents:** Webpack's `webpack.config.js` presets (CRA, Next.js) are Directors — they call a series of configuration builder methods with known-good defaults. ORMs provide `QueryPresets` that encode common query patterns. Test data factory functions (`buildMockUser({ role: 'admin' })`) are lightweight Directors.

sections.title: Builder vs. Options Object vs. Factory: Choosing the Right Tool
sections.content:
The Builder pattern is not always the right choice. Understanding when *not* to use it is as important as knowing when to apply it.

**Plain constructor** — best when the object has 1-3 parameters and all are required. `new Point(x, y)` needs no builder.

**Options object / config object** — best for simple cases with 4-8 optional parameters where no cross-field validation is needed: `createServer({ port: 3000, host: 'localhost', debug: false })`. JavaScript developers are very familiar with this pattern. It requires no extra class, and TypeScript can type-check the object with an interface. Use this when the object is constructed once and never needs presets or Directors.

**Builder pattern** — genuinely earns its extra class when:
1. Many optional parameters (7+) that would make an options object unwieldy.
2. Cross-field validation is needed (rules involving multiple fields).
3. You want step-by-step validation or partial builds.
4. Common construction recipes should be shared across the team (Director).
5. The API should read like natural language: `query.select('name', 'email').from('users').where('age > 18').orderBy('name').limit(10).execute()`.
6. You need to build the same logical thing in multiple representations (e.g., a query builder that can produce SQL or MongoDB syntax from the same chain).

**Factory Method / Abstract Factory** — use when the decision is *which class to instantiate*, not *how to configure one instance*. A factory selects and creates; a builder configures and constructs. They are often combined: a factory method might return a pre-configured builder.

**The overengineering trap:** a `PersonBuilder` with `setFirstName`, `setLastName`, `setAge`, `build()` for an object with three fields is overengineered. The KISS principle applies here: use the simplest thing that works. Builder is a tool for genuinely complex construction, not a ceremony to perform on every class.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: This QueryBuilder mirrors exactly how knex and TypeORM's QueryBuilder work. Multiple `.where()` calls accumulate conditions that are ANDed in `build()`. The Director encodes application-specific query presets. Notice how `.limit()` validates its argument immediately (unlike build() validation) — this is acceptable for single-field rules; build() handles cross-field rules.

sections.title: Advanced Techniques: Cloning, Branching, and Typed Builders
sections.content:
**Cloning for branching builds.** Sometimes you want two variants of a nearly-identical object. Instead of duplicating the entire chain, clone the builder mid-way: `const base = new QueryBuilder('users').select('id', 'email').where('active = true'); const adminQuery = base.clone().where("role = 'admin'").build(); const userQuery = base.clone().where("role = 'user'").build();`. The clone creates a deep copy of the internal config so the two branches are independent. This pattern is extremely common in test suites that create variations of test fixtures.

**Typed builders in TypeScript.** TypeScript can enforce that `build()` is only callable after required fields have been set — using a technique called a *phantom type builder* or *step builder*. Each setter returns a new builder type with the set field marked in a type-level set. `build()` is only available on the type that has all required fields marked. This moves a runtime error into a compile-time error — calling `build()` without a `url` would not compile. This is a powerful technique for public APIs.

**Builder as a configuration accumulator.** Some frameworks use builders not to produce a final object in one shot but to accumulate configuration that is later executed lazily. Mongoose's `Query` object is a builder where `exec()` (equivalent to `build()`) actually sends the database query. The builder accumulates `.find()`, `.sort()`, `.limit()`, `.lean()` calls, then `exec()` serialises the accumulated state into a database wire query.

**Resetting the builder.** If a builder is meant to be reused (e.g., a builder held by a Director), a `reset()` method returns it to its initial state: `reset() { this.#config = { ...this.#defaults }; return this; }`. Call `reset()` after `build()` if you want to construct a new product. Alternatively, always create a fresh builder per product — simpler and less error-prone.

**Builder + Prototype pattern.** In some designs, `clone()` on the Product creates a new builder pre-populated with the product's fields, allowing modification: `const newReq = oldReq.toBuilder().timeout(1000).build()`. This gives you 'with-style updates' on immutable objects — similar to how Kotlin data classes' `copy()` works or how Immer.js handles immutable state updates.

flowchart TD
    A["Builder with\nbase config"] --> B["clone()"] 
    B --> C["Branch 1\n.where admin"]
    B --> D["Branch 2\n.where user"]
    C --> E["build() → adminQuery"]
    D --> F["build() → userQuery"]
    A --> G["Original builder\nunchanged"]
sections.caption: Cloning a partially-configured builder enables two independent branches from a shared base. The original builder is unaffected. This pattern is heavily used in test data factories and A/B variant generation.

sections.title: Builder in Real Frameworks: Pattern Recognition
sections.content:
Once you internalise the Builder pattern, you will see it in virtually every major JavaScript library. Here is a tour of real examples:

**knex.js** — the quintessential query builder: `knex('users').select('id', 'name').where('age', '>', 18).orderBy('name').limit(10)`. Each method (`select`, `where`, `orderBy`, `limit`) is a setter that returns `this`. The terminal step (analogous to `build()`) is implicit when you `await` the chain — knex implements `.then()` on the builder, making it a thenable that executes the query when awaited.

**TypeORM QueryBuilder** — `dataSource.createQueryBuilder('user', 'u').select(['u.id', 'u.email']).where('u.role = :role', { role: 'admin' }).orderBy('u.created_at', 'DESC').getMany()`. Same pattern with `getMany()`, `getOne()`, `getRawMany()` as alternative terminal steps.

**supertest** — HTTP test assertion builder: `request(app).post('/users').send({ name: 'Alice' }).set('Authorization', 'Bearer tok').expect(201).expect('Content-Type', /json/)`. `expect()` is both a setter (accumulating assertions) and a terminal step when called last.

**jest.fn() mock configuration** — `jest.fn().mockReturnValue('foo').mockReturnValueOnce('bar').mockImplementation(() => 'baz')`. Each call accumulates mock behaviour; the mock function object is the Product.

**Mongoose queries** — `User.find({ active: true }).sort({ created_at: -1 }).limit(20).lean().exec()`. `exec()` is the terminal step that sends the query. Without `exec()` (or `await`), the query is just an assembled builder.

**axios request config chaining** — `axios.create({ baseURL, timeout }).interceptors.request.use(...)` is a Director-style preset that customises an axios instance before any requests are made.

**Test data factories (factory-bot, fishery)** — `UserFactory.build({ role: 'admin' })` is a Director method that runs a sequence of builder steps with known defaults, overriding specific fields with the provided options.

**Historical context:** The Builder pattern was formalised in the Gang of Four book (Design Patterns, Gamma et al., 1994) as one of the three creational patterns alongside Factory Method and Abstract Factory. The original motivation was constructing complex document object trees (RTF, PDF) where the same logical document could be rendered in different formats — a single `TextConverter` Director would call methods on either an `RTFBuilder` or a `HTMLBuilder`, producing different outputs from the same construction steps. Modern usage has evolved: the Director is now often implicit (a factory function), and the 'multiple representations from one process' use case has been largely superseded by the 'fluent configuration API' use case. The fluent API angle was popularised by domain-specific languages in the mid-2000s (notably Martin Fowler's work on internal DSLs) and became mainstream in JavaScript with jQuery's chaining API.

**When to use Builder:**
- Object has 6+ optional parameters and callers need to specify only a subset.
- Cross-field validation rules exist (rules spanning multiple fields).
- Common construction recipes should be shared without copy-pasting.
- You want a self-documenting fluent API that reads like English prose.
- The same construction process should produce different output formats.

**When NOT to use Builder:**
- The object has 2-3 fields — use a plain constructor or options object.
- No optional parameters and no cross-field validation — Builder boilerplate is pure overhead.
- The object will be created in a tight loop millions of times — the extra allocation and method calls may matter (profile first).
- You are in a small codebase with no shared presets — the Director overhead is not justified.

**Common mistakes to avoid:**
- Forgetting to clone the config in `build()` — the caller retaining the builder and calling another setter would mutate the 'immutable' product's backing data.
- Putting business logic in setters instead of `build()` — setters should be dumb; validation belongs in `build()`.
- Making the Product mutable — this defeats the purpose of centralised validation.
- Reusing a builder across builds without resetting — stale config from a previous build bleeds into the next product.

items: **Telescoping constructor solved** — the Builder replaces `new Obj(url, null, null, null, 5000, true, null, 3)` with `new ObjBuilder(url).timeout(5000).auth(true).retry(3).build()`. Every parameter is named, optional parameters are omitted cleanly, and call sites are self-documenting.

**Fluent API = method chaining on `this`** — each setter stores its value and returns `this`; the chain reads like a sentence. This is syntactic sugar over sequential method calls on the same mutable builder object.

**`build()` is the single validation gate** — required fields, cross-field constraints, type coercions, and computed defaults all live in `build()`. If `build()` succeeds, the Product is guaranteed valid for its entire lifetime. Partial or invalid products never escape.

**Immutable Product is not optional — it is a correctness guarantee** — `Object.freeze()` ensures that the validation in `build()` cannot be bypassed by post-construction mutation. Immutable products are safe across async boundaries, sharable as cache keys, and free of synchronisation concerns.

**The Director is team knowledge encoded as code** — it encodes common construction recipes so developers call `director.buildAuthenticatedPost(body, token)` instead of remembering the exact sequence of builder calls every time. The Director accepts the builder as a dependency, making it testable and swappable.

**Builder vs. options object** — for objects with 2-5 parameters and no cross-field validation, a plain options object is simpler. Builder earns its boilerplate at 6+ optional parameters, complex validation, or when shared presets (Directors) are needed.

**Every major query library is a Builder** — knex, TypeORM QueryBuilder, Mongoose query chains, supertest, jest mock configuration all implement this pattern. Recognising Builder in libraries makes reading their documentation and debugging their APIs immediately intuitive.

quiz.question: What is the 'telescoping constructor' anti-pattern that the Builder pattern solves?
options: A constructor that recursively calls itself to build nested objects.
A constructor with many optional parameters, forcing callers to pass positional nulls like new Obj(url, null, null, null, 5000).
A constructor that is inherited by too many subclasses, creating a deep hierarchy.
A constructor that reads its configuration from a configuration file at runtime.
quiz.explanation: Telescoping constructor: as optional parameters grow, callers must null-pad positional slots for every field they do not care about. The intent is unreadable, and adding a new parameter breaks every call site. Builder gives each parameter a named setter method instead.

quiz.question: Why does each setter method in a fluent Builder return `this`?
options: To prevent the garbage collector from collecting the builder before build() is called.
To enable method chaining — calling multiple setters in a single expression without intermediate variables.
To signal to the Director that the step completed successfully.
To return the partially-constructed Product after each step.
quiz.explanation: Returning `this` allows chaining: builder.a(1).b(2).c(3).build(). Without it, each setter call would need its own statement. The builder object is returned, not the product — the product only appears after build().

quiz.question: A builder's build() throws 'GET requests cannot have a body' even though both method() and body() individually accepted their arguments. What Builder principle does this demonstrate?
options: Setters should validate their own arguments before storing them.
The Director should reject invalid combinations before passing them to the builder.
build() is the single gate for cross-field validation, where the full accumulated config is visible.
The Product's constructor catches errors that individual setters miss.
quiz.explanation: Cross-field constraints (rules involving two or more fields) cannot be checked in individual setters because each setter only sees one field. build() has the complete accumulated configuration, making it the right place to enforce rules that span multiple fields.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Director's role in the Builder pattern?
options: The Director creates the ConcreteBuilder and owns its lifecycle.
The Director validates the Product after build() completes.
The Director encodes reusable construction recipes by calling a known sequence of builder steps.
The Director is the mandatory entry point — clients must always use a Director, never the builder directly.
quiz.explanation: The Director knows the correct step sequence for common presets (buildAuthenticatedPost, buildHealthCheck). Clients create the builder and pass it to the Director — the Director does not own the builder. Using the builder directly without a Director is equally valid.

quiz.question: Why should the Product produced by build() be immutable (e.g., via Object.freeze())?
options: Immutable objects use less memory because they are pooled by the runtime.
Once build() has validated the configuration, post-construction mutation could put the Product in an invalid state that bypasses validation.
Object.freeze() is required for the Director pattern to function correctly.
Immutability prevents the builder from being reused after build() is called.
quiz.explanation: Mutability after build() lets code bypass the validation gate: req.method = 'INVALID' would work even though build() verified the method. Freezing the Product ensures that if it exists, it passed validation — a permanent invariant that holds across async boundaries and shared references.

quiz.question: You want to build two variants of a query — one for admins and one for regular users — sharing a common base configuration. Which Builder technique enables this?
options: Call build() twice on the same builder — it resets automatically between calls.
Clone the partially-configured builder before diverging, creating two independent branches.
Pass a flag to build() indicating which variant to produce.
Use two separate Directors that each call build() on the same builder.
quiz.explanation: Cloning the builder mid-chain creates an independent copy of the accumulated config. Each clone can then add its own variant-specific steps and call build() independently. Calling build() twice on the same builder would produce the same result unless state is changed between calls.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the most accurate description of knex.js in terms of design patterns?
options: A Factory pattern — it selects which database driver to use based on configuration.
A Builder pattern — each method (select, where, orderBy, limit) accumulates query configuration, and awaiting the chain executes the assembled query.
A Singleton pattern — the knex instance is shared globally across the application.
An Observer pattern — knex listens for database events and reacts to them.
quiz.explanation: knex is a textbook query builder: select(), from(), where(), orderBy(), limit() are setter methods that return the query builder for chaining, and awaiting the result (implicitly calling .then()) is the terminal step equivalent to build(). This is the Builder pattern.

quiz.question: When is a plain options object a better choice than a full Builder class?
options: When the object has more than five fields of any kind.
When the object has 2-3 parameters, no cross-field validation is needed, and no shared Director presets are required.
When the object will be used across async boundaries.
When TypeScript is being used, because TypeScript interfaces replace Builder classes.
quiz.explanation: For simple objects with few parameters and no validation complexity, a plain options object is simpler and clearer than writing a full Builder class. Builder earns its extra boilerplate at 6+ optional parameters, cross-field validation, or when shared presets (Directors) add team-wide value.

quiz.question: How does the Builder pattern differ from Abstract Factory?
options: Builder creates families of related objects; Abstract Factory constructs a single complex object step by step.
Builder constructs one complex object step by step with focus on HOW it is assembled; Abstract Factory creates families of related objects with focus on WHICH class to instantiate.
Builder uses method chaining; Abstract Factory uses inheritance hierarchies.
There is no practical difference — both patterns solve the same problem of object construction.
quiz.explanation: Builder focuses on the construction process of ONE complex object — many steps, detailed configuration, one product. Abstract Factory focuses on creating MULTIPLE related products that form a consistent family, selecting which concrete class to instantiate. Different problem spaces.

quiz.question: A developer builds a builder where each setter immediately validates its own argument, then calls build() with no validation. What problem does this design have?
options: No problem — this is actually a better design because errors are caught earlier.
Cross-field constraints cannot be checked because individual setters only see one field at a time.
This prevents method chaining because validation throws exceptions mid-chain.
The Director will be unable to call build() without triggering validation errors.
quiz.explanation: Individual setters can only validate their own field in isolation. Rules like 'GET cannot have a body' or 'endDate must be after startDate' require knowledge of two or more fields simultaneously. Only build() has the full accumulated configuration, making it the correct home for cross-field validation. Per-setter validation is fine for single-field rules (e.g., 'timeout must be positive') but cannot replace build() validation.
